Chapter 7: Working with Difficult Emotions and Pain
You know, mindfulness really gets put to the test when we're dealing with pain. Whether it’s that stubborn ache in your body, a surge of emotional distress, or those deeper fears that seem to lurk in the background—the first instinct is usually to pull away or try to escape.
But what if you could approach pain differently? Mindfulness invites us to turn toward discomfort—not with harshness or judgment, but with a gentle curiosity.
Now, this isn’t about searching for pain or pretending you don’t want relief. It’s about meeting pain right where it is, just as it is, without piling on self-criticism or extra judgment. When you bring mindful attention to what hurts, you’ll often notice the intensity starts to soften. Suddenly, new pathways for healing can open up.
So, how can you meet pain mindfully?
First, acknowledge the pain. Simply name the sensation or emotion you’re feeling—don’t exaggerate it, but don’t push it away either.
Next, get curious. Where do you feel it in your body? What shape does it take? Just observe—like you’re noticing something for the very first time.
Then, breathe with it. Let your breath anchor you, giving you steady ground while pain is present. This way, the pain’s there, but it doesn’t have to sweep you away.
And finally, offer kindness. Imagine sending a little warmth or compassion right to the spot that hurts. Even a gentle wish for relief can shift how you relate to discomfort.
Let’s make this real with an example. Imagine you’re feeling anxious, and there’s a tightness in your chest. Instead of getting caught up in worry or running from the feeling, you pause. You take a slow breath, and you let yourself notice the tightness—without trying to fix it or push it away. As you pay mindful attention, you might discover that this feeling, while uncomfortable, is actually manageable. And maybe, just maybe, it starts to shift.
One of the most powerful things about mindfulness is learning the difference between pain and suffering. Pain is what you actually feel, physically or emotionally. Suffering? That’s all the extra stuff we layer on—resistance, fear, self-blame. When you face pain directly, you can break that cycle of suffering.
Of course, this isn’t an instant fix. But over time, meeting difficulty with mindfulness helps you build real inner strength and compassion. You start to find more freedom and peace, even when life throws its toughest challenges your way.
